table.title: தமிழ் / বাংলা · Mixed Indic
table.md:
| மொழி | ভাষা | பேசுவோர் | குறிப்பு |
|---|---|---|---|
| தமிழ் | তামিল | 8 கோடி | உலகின் மிகப் பழமையான செம்மொழிகளில் ஒன்றாகக் கருதப்படுகிறது. |
| বাংলা | বাংলা | 23 கோடி | বিশ্বের সপ্তম বৃহত্তম ভাষা, বাংলাদেশ ও পশ্চিমবঙ্গে প্রচলিত। |
| हिन्दी | হিন্দি | 60 கோடி | — |

understanding.purpose: Compare languages by their Tamil and Bengali names, speaker counts, and brief notes.
understanding.reading: Read across each row to connect the two names with the speaker count and note; scan down the speaker column to compare counts.
groups: Columns 1 and 2 give the same language name in two scripts and should have comparable visual weight.
Columns 3 and 4 pair a quantitative speaker count with qualitative context.
keep_intact: Speaker counts as complete values where possible
may_wrap: Notes in column 4 can wrap at word boundaries; their lines can use the height created by other wrapped cells in the same row.

preferred.name: r0A
preferred.note: Give each short column its minimum one-line width and devote the remaining space to the notes.

acceptable.name: r0B
acceptable.note: Give the two language-name columns similar, generous widths while retaining enough space for naturally wrapped notes.

bad.name: r0C
bad.note: Emphasize the speaker-count column for comparison and use a narrower notes column that still fits its longest word.
bad.why: The speaker-count column is much wider than its short values need, while the note column is compressed enough to make the first note five lines tall. The resulting empty space weakens the balance between columns.

rationale: r0A gives the three short identifying and numeric columns enough room to keep their headers and values intact, leaving the largest share for the notes. Both longer notes fit in three lines, so the rows remain compact without breaking words. The other designs devote more space to short entries and make the first note substantially taller.

general: Allocate width according to content and reading role: short labels and values usually need less room than prose.
Preserving words and headers helps scanning, but unused space in one column can force distracting wrapping elsewhere.
specific: The first three columns in r0A are already close to their unbroken header widths, so they have little room to shrink.
The long notes make the fourth column especially sensitive to small reductions in width.

tradeoffs: r0B gives the short columns more breathing room, which some readers may prefer, at the cost of a five-line first note and taller row.
uncertain: The ranges are conservative visual estimates, not browser-tested thresholds. They assume the remaining width is redistributed in roughly the preferred proportions; line breaks can change abruptly near a word boundary.

critique.good: The two language-name columns have comparable visual weight, speaker counts remain intact, and the wider notes column keeps both substantive notes to three lines. The rows read clearly across, with no wrapped headers or split words.
critique.problems: The first three columns are compact, so there is little spare space around their longest entries; the notes still require several lines.
critique.cause: Widths of 73px, 65px and 98px give the first three columns just enough room for their longest unbreakable content. The remaining 243px is allocated to notes.

critique.good: The language names and speaker counts have comfortable horizontal space, and headers and words remain intact.
critique.problems: The first note breaks into five short lines, making its row much taller and leaving conspicuous empty space alongside the name and count. The notes are harder to read as continuous prose.
critique.cause: Increasing the first three columns to 90px, 85px and 105px reduces the notes column to 199px.

critique.good: The two name columns retain a compact, balanced appearance, and the speaker counts are easy to scan.
critique.problems: The speaker column has substantial unused space, while the first note breaks into five lines and creates a tall row with empty space in the other cells.
critique.cause: The 145px speaker column is much wider than its content requires, leaving only 190px for notes.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

ref_equal.why: The notes column is so narrow that Tamil words break awkwardly, making the first row very tall and difficult to read.

ref_auto.why: The compact identifier and count columns leave generous room for notes; text stays intact and rows are easy to scan.

r0B.why: The columns are balanced and text remains intact, though the narrower notes column creates more wrapping and taller rows than necessary.

r0A.why: The first three columns fit their content closely, giving the notes room to wrap naturally while keeping rows easy to compare.

r0C.why: The count column has substantial unused space while the notes wrap into several lines, weakening the balance between columns.

raw.unsure: B and D appear visually indistinguishable at this resolution; any small difference in their column widths is not apparent.

r0A.why: The compact language and speaker columns leave generous space for the notes. Headers and values remain intact, and the rows are easy to scan.

ref_auto.why: The columns fit their contents closely, giving the notes enough room to wrap naturally while keeping each row easy to follow.

r0B.why: The language and speaker columns have surplus space, leaving the notes narrow. The Tamil note runs to five lines, making the first row tall.

r0C.why: The speaker column is unusually wide for its short values, while the narrow note column creates a tall first row and uneven white space.

ref_equal.why: The first three columns consume too much width, squeezing the notes into a narrow strip. Words break across lines and the rows become excessively tall.

raw.unsure: A and B appear nearly identical at this image scale; any difference between them is too slight to rank reliably.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
